hints: Recall whether barium hydroxide is more or less soluble than magnesium hydroxide to state the trend down Group 2.
Think of dissolving as two steps, breaking the lattice apart and then hydrating the gaseous ions, and consider how both enthalpy changes vary with ionic size.
Compare the size of the $\text{OH}^{-}$ ion with the $\text{M}^{2+}$ ions to decide which enthalpy, lattice or hydration, is more sensitive to the growing cation.
Link the balance of those two enthalpy changes to $\Delta H_{sol}$ and hence to why solubility changes in that direction.
walkthrough:
Picture what solubility means here**
Think of solid $\text{M(OH)}_2$ breaking into $\text{M}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and $2\text{OH}^{-}(\text{aq})$. Magnesium hydroxide is almost insoluble, calcium hydroxide is sparingly soluble, while barium hydroxide is much more soluble. So solubility increases going down Group 2.

Split dissolving into two energy steps**
Imagine first pulling the lattice apart into gaseous ions, that costs energy equal to $-\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$, then letting water surround the gaseous ions, that releases $\Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}$. Overall $$\Delta H_{sol}^{\ominus} = -\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus} + \Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}$$ Both $\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}$ are negative, and both become less negative down the group because the $\text{M}^{2+}$ ion gets larger and charge density falls.

See why lattice wins the race**
Lattice strength depends on both ions, $\text{M}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$, while hydration of the cation depends mainly on $\text{M}^{2+}$. Because $\text{OH}^{-}$ is very small, increasing the cation size has a proportionally larger effect on the lattice. So $\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$ falls in magnitude faster than $\Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}$.

Connect to $\Delta H_{sol}$**
Less energy is needed to break the weaker lattice, but almost as much energy is still released on hydration. The balance shifts so $\Delta H_{sol}^{\ominus}$ becomes more negative, less positive, down the group. A more exothermic solution enthalpy drives the equilibrium toward dissolved ions, so solubility increases.

Final answer: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group.
Both $\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}$ become less exothermic down the group.
$\Delta H_{latt}^{\ominus}$ decreases more rapidly than $\Delta H_{hyd}^{\ominus}$ because $\text{OH}^{-}$ is small compared to $\text{M}^{2+}$.
Therefore $\Delta H_{sol}^{\ominus}$ becomes more exothermic / less endothermic down the group, favouring dissolving.

hints: Write the expression $\Delta H_{r}^{\ominus} = \sum \Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(\text{reactants})$ and remember that $\text{Ba(OH)}_2(\text{aq})$ means $\text{Ba}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{OH}^{-}(\text{aq})$.
Substitute the table values carefully, noting the factor of 2 for $\text{OH}^{-}$, then evaluate products minus reactants.
walkthrough:
Build the formation values for each side**
For reaction 1: $$\text{Ba(OH)}_2(\text{aq}) + \text{CO}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{BaCO}_3(\text{s}) + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$$ $\text{Ba(OH)}_2(\text{aq})$ is fully ionised, so $$\Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}[\text{Ba(OH)}_2(\text{aq})] = -538 + 2(-230) = -998 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Apply products minus reactants**
Products: $$(-1216) + (-286) = -1502 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Reactants: $$(-998) + (-394) = -1392 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ So $$\Delta H_{r1}^{\ominus} = -1502 - (-1392) = -110 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The negative sign shows the precipitation is exothermic.

hints: Write $\Delta H_{r2}^{\ominus}$ as formation enthalpies of products minus reactants, letting $y = \Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}[\text{HCO}_{3}^{-}(\text{aq})]$ so that $\text{Ba(HCO}_{3})_{2}(\text{aq})$ contributes $-538 + 2y$.
Substitute $\Delta H_{r2}^{\ominus} = -26 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and the known table values, then solve the linear equation for $y$.
walkthrough:
Set up the unknown**
Reaction 2: $$\text{BaCO}_3(\text{s}) + \text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{Ba(HCO}_3)_2(\text{aq})$$ Let $$y = \Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}[\text{HCO}_{3}^{-}(\text{aq})]$$ Then $$\Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}[\text{Ba(HCO}_3)_2(\text{aq})] = -538 + 2y$$ because it contains one $\text{Ba}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and two $\text{HCO}_{3}^{-}(\text{aq})$.

hints: Apply products minus reactants to reaction 3 using your value of $-692 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for $\text{HCO}_{3}^{-}(\text{aq})$ together with the table values for $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, $\text{OH}^{-}$ and $\text{CO}_{2}$.
walkthrough:
Combine the data in one step**
Reaction 3: $$\text{Ba(OH)}_2(\text{aq}) + 2\text{CO}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{Ba(HCO}_3)_2(\text{aq})$$ Products: $$-538 + 2(-692) = -1922 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Reactants: $$[-538 + 2(-230)] + 2(-394) = -998 - 788 = -1786 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Difference: $$\Delta H_{r3}^{\ominus} = -1922 - (-1786) = -136 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Notice this also equals $\Delta H_{r1}^{\ominus} + \Delta H_{r2}^{\ominus} = -110 + (-26)$.

hints: Write the full ionic equation for reaction 3 and for reaction 4 and see what happens to $\text{Ba}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{aq})$.
Consider whether the metal ion appears in a different state on each side or remains unchanged in solution, and what that implies for $\Delta H$.
walkthrough:
Cancel the spectators**
Expand reaction 3: $$\text{Ba}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{OH}^{-}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{CO}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{Ba}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{HCO}_{3}^{-}(\text{aq})$$ $\text{Ba}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ appears identically on both sides. The same is true for $\text{Ca}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ in reaction 4.

See the common chemistry**
Cancelling gives the same net ionic equation: $$2\text{OH}^{-}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{CO}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow 2\text{HCO}_{3}^{-}(\text{aq})$$ Since the bonds broken and made are identical and the spectator ions undergo no change, $\Delta H_{r}^{\ominus}$ is the same for the calcium and barium versions.

Final answer: $\Delta H_{r3}^{\ominus}$ will be identical to $\Delta H_{r4}^{\ominus}$ / unchanged.
The net ionic reaction is the same in both cases: $2\text{OH}^{-}(\text{aq}) + 2\text{CO}_{2}(\text{g}) \rightarrow 2\text{HCO}_{3}^{-}(\text{aq})$, the metal ions $\text{M}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ are spectators and remain in solution.

hints: Count the moles of gas consumed in reaction 1 compared with reaction 3, remembering that gases have far higher entropy than solids, liquids or aqueous ions.
Relate loss of gas moles to the sign and magnitude of $\Delta S^{\ominus}$, more gas lost means a larger decrease in disorder.
walkthrough:
Compare the gas stoichiometry**
Reaction 1 uses $1$ mol of $\text{CO}_2(\text{g})$: $$\text{Ba(OH)}_2(\text{aq}) + \text{CO}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{BaCO}_3(\text{s}) + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$$ Reaction 3 uses $2$ mol: $$\text{Ba(OH)}_2(\text{aq}) + 2\text{CO}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{Ba(HCO}_3)_2(\text{aq})$$

Link gas loss to entropy**
Gases are highly disordered. Removing gas from the system causes a large drop in entropy. Because reaction 3 removes twice as much gas with no gas produced, disorder falls further. So $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ for reaction 3 is more negative than for reaction 1.

Final answer: Reaction 3 consumes more moles of gas / more $\text{CO}_{2}(\text{g})$ than reaction 1 (2 mol versus 1 mol).
Therefore $\Delta S_{r3}^{\ominus}$ is expected to be more negative / less positive than $\Delta S_{r1}^{\ominus}$.
